description: Spaced-repetition state per concept. Each entry tracks SM-2 (ease_factor / interval / repetitions / next_due) plus all attempts.

attempts.question: A junior engineer on your team is starting a greenfield agentic project and their first move is to pick the model — they're benchmarking GPT-5 vs Claude vs Gemini before anything else. What's the one thing you push back on, and what should they be doing instead?
attempts.canonical_answer: Stop. Picking the model first is the classic determinism-ladder inversion, and it's the failure mode I've watched burn whole teams. Once you've committed to a frontier model, every architectural choice downstream — your tool surface, your context budget, your retry semantics, your eval harness — gets constrained by that model's quirks. You've spent your autonomy budget before you've defined the problem. The ladder runs the other way: start at the most deterministic rung you can tolerate. Can this be a SQL query? A typed function? A constrained DSL? A small fine-tuned classifier? Only climb to a general-purpose LLM when the rung below genuinely can't carry the load. Every lever — schema constraints, tool whitelists, structured outputs, model size, temperature, agentic loops — trades autonomy for determinism, and you want to be spending autonomy deliberately, not by default. Concrete example: I've seen a team use GPT-4 to extract dates from invoices. A regex and a date library shipped in two days, ran for free, and never hallucinated a fiscal quarter.

attempts.question: A teammate proposes building a custom MCP server so the agent can list S3 buckets, query a Postgres table, and hit one internal REST endpoint. They've already sketched the protocol handlers. What's the one thing you push back on before they write another line of code, and how do you frame the alternative?
attempts.canonical_answer: I stop them at the protocol handlers. The pushback is simple: you're reaching for the heaviest lever in the stack to solve a problem the lightest lever already closes. MCP is real infrastructure — auth, lifecycle, schema, version drift, a server you now own forever. For three read-only calls, six lines of system prompt plus a shell tool or a thin function wrapper does the same job and you can delete it on a Friday without a migration. The named failure mode is over-leveraging: paying MCP-tier complexity cost for prompt-tier value. The decision lever is, walk up the stack — prompt, then tool function, then RAG, then fine-tune, then MCP — and stop at the first rung that actually closes the gap. I lost three weeks once building an MCP server for `aws s3 ls`. Six lines of system prompt would have shipped it Monday. Smallest lever wins. You can always graduate up; you rarely get the weeks back.

attempts.question: A teammate proposes building a custom MCP server so the agent can list S3 buckets, read CloudWatch logs, and tail RDS slow queries. They've already scoped two sprints. What's the one thing you push back on before they write a line of code, and how do you frame the alternative?
attempts.canonical_answer: Push back on the assumption that 'agent needs to do X' implies 'we need to build a tool for X.' That's the failure mode smallest-lever-wins guards against — reaching for the heaviest mechanism (custom tool, MCP server, fine-tune) when a lighter lever closes the gap. The lever ordering is roughly: prompt > example in context > retrieval > existing tool > new tool > fine-tune. You only descend when the layer above demonstrably fails, not speculatively. For the S3/CloudWatch/RDS case: nine times out of ten you can put six lines in the system prompt telling the agent to shell out to the AWS CLI through an existing exec tool, and you're done in an afternoon. I burned three weeks once building an MCP server for `aws s3 ls` that should have been a system-prompt instruction — the cost wasn't just the three weeks, it was the maintenance surface I now own forever. Make them prove the prompt-level fix fails before greenlighting the server.
